sections.b: Matthew opens the New Testament with a family list that runs forward from Abraham through David and the kings of Judah, through the exile, to "Jesus, the one called the Messiah" (Matthew 1:1–17). He arranges it in three sets of fourteen, perhaps because the Hebrew letters of David's name add up to fourteen, and he leaves out kings to make the pattern (Matthew 1:8). He names four women, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Uriah's wife, and breaks his own pattern at the end: Joseph does not father Jesus; Jesus is born from Mary (Matthew 1:16). Luke's list (Luke 3:23–38) runs backward to Adam through David's son Nathan and names a different father for Joseph, which readers explain by levirate marriage, by Luke giving Mary's line, or by each writer's purpose.

common: Matthew's genealogy proves Jesus' physical descent from David through Joseph.
uncommon: The three fourteens make six sevens, so Jesus opens the seventh and final age of history.

sections.b: Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side. Mary, legally betrothed to Joseph, is "discovered to be pregnant from the Holy Spirit" before they live together (Matthew 1:18). Joseph plans a quiet divorce, but an angel in a dream tells him the child is from the Spirit and that he must name him Jesus (Matthew 1:20–21). Matthew sees here the fulfillment of Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form, "the virgin will be pregnant" (Matthew 1:23), and stresses that Joseph did not sleep with Mary before the birth (Matthew 1:25). Luke tells the story independently from Mary's side (Luke 1:26–38). Traditional Christians confess it in the creeds; some historians call it historically unresolvable; Jewish critics from the 100s answered with a charge of illegitimacy.

uncommon: Matthew's four women in the genealogy are meant to prepare readers for a birth that would look scandalous.

sections.b: In Matthew, Mary never speaks. She is "his mother Mary," promised in marriage to Joseph and found pregnant from the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18); the magi find "the child and Mary, his mother" (Matthew 2:11); Joseph takes "the child and his mother" to Egypt and back (Matthew 2:13–21). Matthew's "until she had a son" (Matthew 1:25) is the center of the debate over whether Mary remained a virgin: the Greek heōs hou does not by itself say what happened afterward, and churches answer differently (see the card on Matthew 1).
sections.refs: Matthew 1:16; Matthew 1:18–25; Matthew 2:11; Matthew 2:13–21; Matthew 12:46–50; Matthew 13:55

sections.b: "Magi from the east" arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews, whose star they saw "at its rising" (Matthew 2:1–2). After Herod's scholars point them to Bethlehem, the star goes before them to the house, where they bow down to the child and give gold, frankincense and myrrh (Matthew 2:9–11), then go home by another road after a dream (Matthew 2:12). Magi were Persian priestly sages and star-watchers; Matthew does not say how many there were or call them kings. Tradition made them three because of the gifts, kings because of Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3–6, and gave them names in the 500s. For Matthew they are the first Gentiles to honor Jesus, a hint of the mission to all nations (Matthew 28:19).

Proposals include a miracle, the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in 7 BC (Kepler), a comet recorded by Chinese astronomers in 5 BC (Humphreys), and an astrological sign in Aries in 6 BC (Molnar). Many readers link it with Balaam's oracle, "A star will march out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:17). A star that moves ahead of travelers and stops over a house is not easily explained by astronomy.

common: There were three kings named Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, who visited the manger.
uncommon: The magi were Jewish or God-fearing astrologers from the Jewish community in Babylon.

sections.h: Herod the Great and Archelaus in Matthew 2
sections.b: Matthew sets Jesus' birth "while Herod was king" (Matthew 2:1), which points to about 6–4 BC, since Herod died in 4 BC. Alarmed by the magi's question, Herod plots to find the child and kills the boys of Bethlehem two years old and under (Matthew 2:16). No other ancient source mentions this, but it fits the suspicious cruelty Josephus records, including the killing of three of his own sons. After Herod's death his son Archelaus ruled Judea (4 BC–AD 6) so harshly that Augustus removed him, and Joseph avoids Judea and settles in Galilee under Herod Antipas (Matthew 2:22).

sections.h: John's preaching and baptism in Matthew 3
sections.b: Matthew presents John as the voice of Isaiah 40:3 and dresses him like Elijah (Matthew 3:3–4; 2 Kings 1:8). His message is the same as Jesus' first preaching: "Repent, because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near" (Matthew 3:2; Matthew 4:17). He baptizes crowds from Jerusalem and Judea in the Jordan as they confess their sins, warns the Pharisees and Sadducees that descent from Abraham is no shelter, and points to a stronger one who will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:5–12). Only Matthew reports John's protest when Jesus comes to be baptized and Jesus' answer, "to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:14–15). When John is "handed over," Jesus begins his work in Galilee (Matthew 4:12).

common: John lived at Qumran as a member of the Essene community.

sections.b: John's baptism in the Jordan was a once-for-all immersion tied to repentance and the confession of sins in view of the coming judgment (Matthew 3:6, 11). Jews knew purity washings, but John's rite was new: given by him, once, in a river, to Israelites. Jesus' own baptism by John (Matthew 3:13–17) became the pattern and the ground of Christian baptism in the eyes of most churches, though they differ on how John's baptism relates to Christian baptism: Trent denied they had the same effect, while Calvin held they were the same sacrament. Baptists see in Jesus coming "up from the water" (Matthew 3:16) the model of believer's baptism by immersion.

Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and forty nights, like Moses on the mountain, and is tested by the devil (Matthew 4:1–2). The tester takes up the voice from heaven, "If you are God's Son," and tempts him to turn stones to bread, to throw himself from the Temple and dare God to save him (quoting Psalm 91:11–12), and to worship him in exchange for the world's kingdoms (Matthew 4:3–9). Jesus answers each time from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses' words about Israel's forty years: people live by God's word, do not put God to the test, and worship God alone (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Where Israel failed in the wilderness, God's Son is faithful. Luke has the same tests with the Temple last (Luke 4:1–13); Mark summarizes in two verses (Mark 1:12–13).
sections.refs: Matthew 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 6:13; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 8:2–3; Luke 4:1–13; Mark 1:12–13; Hebrews 4:15

common: The devil's three temptations correspond to the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life in 1 John 2:16.

sections.b: After John is handed over, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and makes his home in Capernaum by the lake (Matthew 4:12–13). Matthew quotes Isaiah 9:1–2: the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first to fall to Assyria in 733 BC, "Galilee of the nations," is the first to see a great light (Matthew 4:15–16). From there Jesus teaches in the synagogues, proclaims the good news of the kingdom and heals, and crowds come from all of Galilee and beyond (Matthew 4:23–25). Galilee was mostly Jewish in Jesus' day, ruled by Herod Antipas and surrounded by Gentile cities.

Matthew has Joseph settle the family in Nazareth after the return from Egypt and adds, "so that what was spoken through the prophets would be fulfilled: 'He will be called a Nazarene'" (Matthew 2:23). No Old Testament verse says this. The most common explanation is a wordplay on netser, the "shoot" from Jesse's roots in Isaiah 11:1; others suggest the Nazirite of Judges 13:5, or the despised Messiah of Isaiah 53, since Nazareth was an obscure village (John 1:46).

Matthew and Luke agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:4–7). In Matthew, Herod's chief priests and scribes find it in Micah 5:2, joined with God's word to David, "You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2), and Matthew changes Micah's "too small" to "in no way the least" (Matthew 2:5–6). The boys of Bethlehem are killed by Herod, and Matthew hears in it Rachel weeping, whose tomb tradition placed near the town (Matthew 2:16–18; Genesis 35:19).

Ten times Matthew interrupts his story to say that something happened "so that what was spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22–23; Matthew 2:15; Matthew 2:17–18; Matthew 2:23; Matthew 4:14–16; Matthew 8:17; Matthew 12:17–21; Matthew 13:35; Matthew 21:4–5; Matthew 27:9–10). Several are not predictions in their first setting but patterns: Hosea 11:1 speaks of Israel brought out of Egypt, and Matthew applies it to Jesus (Matthew 2:15); Jeremiah 31:15 is Rachel weeping over the exiles, which Matthew hears again at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18). For Matthew, Jesus relives and completes Israel's story: down to Egypt, out through the water, tested in the wilderness, teaching from a mountain like Moses.
sections.refs: Matthew 1:22–23; Matthew 2:15; Matthew 2:17–18; Matthew 4:1–11; Hosea 11:1; Jeremiah 31:15

sections.h: Jesus' childhood as a new exodus
sections.b: Matthew tells Jesus' early life in the shape of Moses' story and Israel's exodus. A king kills the Hebrew boys, and the child escapes (Matthew 2:13–16; Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:15). The family returns when "the ones who wanted the child's life have died" (Matthew 2:20), echoing God's word to Moses (Exodus 4:19). "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Matthew 2:15) recalls Israel as God's firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). Then Jesus passes through the water (Matthew 3:16) and is tested forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11).
sections.refs: Matthew 2:13–23; Exodus 1:22; Exodus 2:15; Exodus 4:19–22; Hosea 11:1; Matthew 3:16; Matthew 4:1–11

sections.h: "The kingdom of heaven has drawn near"
sections.b: Matthew usually writes "the kingdom of heaven," a reverent Jewish way of saying "kingdom of God." It means God's reign, not a place in the sky. John the Baptist and Jesus open their preaching with the same words: "Repent, because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near" (Matthew 3:2; Matthew 4:17). Jesus' work of teaching and healing is "the good news of the kingdom" (Matthew 4:23), echoing Isaiah's messenger who tells Zion, "Your God is King!" (Isaiah 52:7).

sections.h: The first word of John and Jesus
sections.b: "Repent" (metanoeite, "change your mind," carrying the Hebrew sense of turning back to God) is the first word of John's preaching and of Jesus' (Matthew 3:2; Matthew 4:17). John demands "fruit worthy of repentance" (Matthew 3:8). The Latin "do penance" for this word became part of the Reformation debate; Luther's first thesis (1517) says Christ meant the whole life of believers to be repentance.

At Jesus' baptism a voice from heaven announces, "This is my dearly loved Son; in him I take delight" (Matthew 3:17), joining Psalm 2:7 (the king as God's son), Isaiah 42:1 (the servant) and Genesis 22:2 (Isaac, the loved son). Matthew has already applied Hosea's "Out of Egypt I called my son" to Jesus (Matthew 2:15). At once the devil tests the meaning of the title: "If you are God's Son" (Matthew 4:3, 6).
sections.refs: Matthew 2:15; Matthew 3:17; Matthew 4:3; Matthew 4:6; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Genesis 22:2

sections.h: John the Baptist dressed as Elijah
sections.b: Matthew describes John's camel-hair garment and leather belt (Matthew 3:4) in words that recall Elijah, "a hairy man ... with a leather loincloth tied around his waist" (2 Kings 1:8). Malachi had promised that God would send Elijah before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and Jesus later says John is that Elijah (Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12–13). Jesus' call of the fishermen also echoes Elijah's call of Elisha from his plowing (1 Kings 19:19–21; Matthew 4:18–22).
sections.refs: Matthew 3:4; 2 Kings 1:8; Malachi 4:5; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12–13; 1 Kings 19:19–21

sections.b: After Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem, Matthew quotes Jeremiah 31:15: "A cry was heard in Ramah ... Rachel is weeping for her children" (Matthew 2:18). In Jeremiah, Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps as her descendants go into exile, and God at once promises their return. Matthew may have been helped by the tradition that Rachel was buried "on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem" (Genesis 35:19).

Jesus fasts "for forty days and forty nights" in the wilderness before his testing (Matthew 4:2), like Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9) and Elijah on his way to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). The forty days became the model for Lent in the churches, kept in different ways or not at all (see the card on Matthew 4).

In Matthew 4 the devil (diabolos, "slanderer") is called "the tester" (Matthew 4:3) and finally "Satan" (Matthew 4:10). He quotes Scripture (Psalm 91:11–12) and claims to be able to give all the world's kingdoms (Matthew 4:8–9). Jesus dismisses him, "Go away, Satan!", the same rebuke he later gives Peter when Peter tries to turn him from the cross (Matthew 16:23).

sections.h: John and Jesus in the wilderness
sections.b: John preaches in the Judean wilderness as the voice of Isaiah 40:3 (Matthew 3:1–3), and Jesus is led there by the Spirit to be tested forty days (Matthew 4:1–2). Both scenes call up Israel's forty years in the wilderness, where God led, fed and tested his people (Deuteronomy 8:2), and the prophets' promise of a new exodus starting in the desert.

sections.h: Birth, baptism and the first call (Matthew 1–4)
sections.b: Matthew introduces Jesus as "son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1), born in Bethlehem in Herod's last years to Mary, betrothed to Joseph, and conceived by the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18–2:1). He is named Jesus, "for he is the one who will save his people from their sins," and Immanuel, "God is with us" (Matthew 1:21–23). After the flight to Egypt he grows up in Nazareth (Matthew 2:23), is baptized by John and named by the voice from heaven as God's Son (Matthew 3:13–17), is tested in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), and begins preaching the kingdom in Galilee from his base in Capernaum, calling his first disciples (Matthew 4:12–22).

Matthew opens with words that echo Genesis, "The book of the family history" (Matthew 1:1; Genesis 5:1), and builds his first four chapters as a prologue: who Jesus is (son of David, son of Abraham, Immanuel, God's Son), where he comes from (Bethlehem, Egypt, Nazareth, Galilee), and how his work begins. Five fulfillment quotations in these chapters set the pattern of the book, and Joseph's obedient dreams, the magi's search and the first disciples' call show what response to Jesus looks like.
